question: At the international level, the World Health Organization (WHO), followed by the American Medical Association in 2013, have already recognised obesity as a chronic disease. According to Eurostat, over half of adults in the EU (50.6 %) are overweight, with 17 % suffering from obesity.

According to the 2022 WHO European Regional Obesity Report, obesity has been linked to at least 13 types of cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular and musculoskeletal disease, as well as mental health disorders. The Blueprint for Action to Address Obesity estimates the annual cost of obesity at approximately EUR 70 billion.

Despite the European Association for the Study of Obesity (EASO) advocating for the recognition of obesity at the EU level and Parliament calling on the Commission to align with the 11th Revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11) in its resolution of December 20231, the recognition, diagnosis, and treatment of obesity remain fragmented across the EU. 1.
Does the Commission intend to recognise obesity as a chronic disease under European public health policy, and through which policy instruments and, if so, on what timeframe?
How does the Commission intend to support Member States in improving the recognition, research, and treatment of obesity?
Does the Commission intend to address the discrimination against persons suffering from obesity, particularly children affected by bullying, both offline and online?
Resolution of 13 December 2023 on non-communicable diseases (NCDs) (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/C/2024/4171/oj). 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.8.2026) Under Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU1, Member States are responsible for organising and delivering their health services. The Commission supports Member States in addressing non-communicable diseases (NCDs) and their risk factors, including obesity, through the ‘Healthier Together’ EU NCD initiative2.

The EU4Health Programme3 funds actions that address obesity, such as the joint actions PreventNCD4 and Health4EUkids5, and stakeholder-led projects such as PODiaCar6. The Safe Hearts Plan7 builds on these actions under its prevention pillar. The Health Promotion and Disease Prevention Knowledge Gateway8 provides information on primary prevention programmes and policy recommendations related to obesity prevention.

Through the Horizon Europe programme9 over EUR 2.7 billion have been invested in research and innovation related to obesity, diabetes and nutrition. The EU Funding and Tenders Portal10 includes information about open and upcoming funding opportunities for related research. In February 2026, the Commission adopted the Action Plan against cyberbullying11.

It sets out complementary measures to address abusive behaviour online through protection, prevention, support for victims and improved reporting mechanisms, including appearance-related cyberbullying affecting children and young people. In line with the Commission Recommendation on integrated child protection systems12, it calls for national comprehensive anti-bullying plans.
The World Health Organization is responsible for the International Classification of Diseases13 (ICD-11). The Commission has no role in this process.
